doctitle: Lesson-Plan Implementation Guide — Critical Thinking Online Breakouts
h1: Building a Lesson Around a Breakout
lead: A ready structure for slotting a Critical Thinking Online Breakout into a full lesson, following a standard Texas lesson-plan format. Use the outline below as-is, or copy the field list into your campus template. A worked example for this suite appears at the end.
howto: 🧑‍🏫 How to use this guide: a breakout works best as the engage or collaborative practice phase of a lesson — not the whole lesson. The sections below mirror a standard lesson plan; each one names what to decide and how the breakout fits. Pair it with the UDL and ELPS supports pages for the differentiation section.
s1.p: Record the essentials so the plan is reusable and reviewable: teacher, campus/district, grade level, course/subject, unit, lesson title, date, duration, instructional setting (whole group / small group / centers / lab / online / blended), number of students, and prerequisite skills or prior learning. A single breakout typically fits a 20–40 minute block.
s2.p: Name the primary standard the breakout targets and pull the exact citation from the standards correlation guide for this suite. Add the ELPS for your emergent bilingual students (listening, speaking, reading, writing) and a language objective. List any crosswalk standards your campus requires.
s3.p: State the big idea / concept the breakout reveals, one or two essential questions, and a short rationale — why this matters and how it connects to the unit or the real world.
s4.p: Write measurable objectives for the end of the lesson: a content objective (“Students will…”), a language objective if applicable (“Students will use language to…”), and success criteria students can check themselves against (“I know I am successful when I can…”). Solving all four locks is a natural, visible success marker.
s5.p: Pre-teach the two or three terms the breakout hinges on. Where the suite includes a word bank or glossary, use it. Provide student-friendly definitions, a visual, and sentence stems for discussion — for example, “This clue tells me ___, so the lock is ___.”
s6.p: Technology: one device per student or pair, a modern browser, and the breakout link — no login and no data collected. Optional: a projector to model the first lock, headphones for read-aloud, and printed clue cards for offline groups. List any teacher and student materials your lesson adds around the activity.
s7.p: Before (activator): a quick prompt or image to surface prior knowledge and misconceptions. During (formative): circulate and listen — which clue are pairs using, where do they stall, how do they handle the decoy? The “locks open” count is a live progress check. After (product): an exit task — students explain in one or two sentences how they cracked one lock, or answer a transfer question.
s8.p: Plan universal supports first: engagement (choice of language and partner, playful retry), representation (seven languages, chunked clue cards, word bank), and action & expression (four different response modes). Add emergent-bilingual and special-education supports as needed. See the dedicated UDL supports and ELPS supports pages for specific moves by principle and proficiency level.
s9.intro: A workable arc that places the breakout at the center. Adjust the timing to your block.
p1.h: Hook and set the goal (5 min)
p1.b: Pose the essential question with an image or quick prompt. Preview the vocabulary and show the 🌐 language menu. Name the goal: open all four locks using the clues.
p2.b: Project the breakout and think aloud through the first clue and one lock. Show how to reopen clues and how “Start over” works. Make the decoy idea explicit: a clue can be true and still not help.
p3.b: Two students per device. Partners read each clue, decide which lock it serves, and justify their choice out loud before answering. Circulate and ask “which clue, which lock, why.” This is the formative-assessment window.
p4.b: Students replay in a second language, try a related breakout from the concept set, or answer a short transfer prompt on their own.
p5.b: Students answer: What did you learn? How does it connect to what you already knew? Where else could you use this idea? Debrief the decoy as a class.
s10.list:
• Recall: What does this clue say? Which lock does it match?
  • Reasoning: Why does this clue open that lock and not another?
  • Transfer: Where else would this idea be true?
  • Misconceptions: Why is the decoy clue true but not helpful here?
s11.list:
• What worked, and what evidence showed students learned?
  • Who needs reteaching, and who is ready for extension?
  • Which clue or lock caused the most productive struggle?
  • What will you change next time?
ex.lang: Students will explain, using a sentence stem, which clue opened each lock and why.
ex.success: I can open all four locks and explain the clue-to-lock reasoning for at least two of them.
disc: This guide is a planning aid, not an official lesson plan. Adapt it to your campus template and confirm standards before adoption.
